report.source_text: A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was performed at the referring hospital, and it showed a segment of circumferential wall thickening affecting the proximal descending colon, 6.3 cm long, with a maximum wall thickness of 1.6 cm. Peri-colonic fat stranding and multifocal regional nodules and lymph nodes were identified. Multiple peritoneal deposits were seen, and the largest deposit was seen along the mesenteric margin, measuring 4.9×3 cm. There was no definitive involvement of adjacent structures. There were innumerable hypovascular ring-enhancing hepatic masses scattered in both lobes involving all liver segments, and the largest was located at segment 4b, measuring 8.1 cm. There was also necrotic lymphadenopathy seen at the gastrohepatic ligament.

report.source_text: Histopathological examination of the descending colon biopsy demonstrated dual morphologies in which a predominant component comprised of tumor cells arranged in nested, organoid, and rosette-like growth patterns with a focal area of solid sheet associated with brisk mitotic activity estimated at 30 mitotic figures per 10 high-powered fields (Figure 3A). The second minor component (30%) exhibited intermingled malignant glandular structures morphologically consistent with adenocarcinoma (Figure 3B). The predominant component was diffusely positive for Pancytokeratin (AE1/AE3) and Synaptophysin and negative for Chromogranin immunohisto-chemical stains, whereas adenocarcinoma was negative for the neuroendocrine markers (Figure 3C, 3D).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 48-year-old man with diabetes and ulcerative colitis presented with right upper quadrant pain, weight loss, constipation, and a palpable epigastric mass. CT imaging revealed circumferential wall thickening of the proximal descending colon with regional lymphadenopathy, multiple peritoneal deposits, and widespread hypovascular hepatic masses consistent with metastases. Colonoscopic biopsy of the colon lesion confirmed a poorly differentiated mixed adenoneuroendocrine carcinoma (MANEC) by demonstrating dual morphologies and immunohistochemical positivity for neuroendocrine markers. Although a liver biopsy was ordered to confirm metastatic involvement, the diagnosis of metastatic MANEC was established on radiological and histopathological findings correlating the colon primary with metastatic lesions.
